chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
title: Escalating Capitol contract with royalties and the Dakota Staton date
summary: Burke wrote a royalty-bearing contract, as Jones had never been paid royalties on earlier records, and Capitol had him accompany Dakota Staton on the hit "The Late, Late Show".

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: And that makes me die for the guy, you know. He's just one of the family to me. And now he gives it back to him, and then we start manoeuvering with Capitol to get a contract that escalates, and royalties. I've been making records all my life, never got no royalties. I took all the contracts and things that I'd signed with different records, with Angel Records, that stuff I made with Angel, never got a nickel for none of the stuff, or Commodore or nothing. So Sammy said, "All this has got to quit now. This has got to quit." So he figures out a contract escalating the money and so first they got -- I think Dave is just getting his foot in the door, but he gets Dakota Staton. So he has -- he says, "I want you to make a record date with Dakota." Okay. Van Alexander's going to make the arrangements, and Milt will be on there and O and Jimmy Cleveland, trombone player, and some old guys. So we did, we went down and made the record, Late, Late Show, and Hank Jones on piano, and big. The thing sold like anything, sold big.
They had good promotion at that time.
